description: I’m Vivek, a B.Tech CSE (Data Science) student and freelance full-stack developer (React, Node, Gemini API) with a passion for physics and quantum mechanics. I'm leading 'Team Solar system' to tackle the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by building an AI-powered interactive 3D map using NASA datasets. I'm looking for creative UI/UX designers, 3D graphics developers (like Three.js), and space data enthusiasts to round out the team. Let's build an award-winning app together!
summary:
We built the **Lunar Landing Site Navigator**, a web app designed to make planning moon missions much more intuitive.

To address the challenge, we took complex NASA SPICE data and 3D terrain maps and connected them to an easy-to-use interactive Mission Planner. Instead of wrestling with raw numbers, users can simply pick a location on the Moon, set a timeframe, and let the app instantly calculate critical details like lighting conditions, surface slopes, and overall terrain safety.

This matters because orbital mechanics and planetary data are usually incredibly difficult to decode. Our project bridges that gap. It turns heavy, scientifically rigorous data into a visual, accessible platform, empowering everyone—from actual mission architects to passionate space fans—to explore, validate, and strategize safe lunar landings without needing a PhD in astrophysics.
details:
What it does and how it works The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is essentially a smart map and mission simulator for the Moon. You enter specific coordinates and a time frame into our web interface, and the app calculates exactly what the conditions will be like at that spot. Under the hood, the web app sends your request to a custom-built Python "science engine." This engine crunches real NASA SPICE kernels (which track planetary orbits and positions) and 3D elevation models to determine the lighting, terrain slope, and overall safety of the landing zone at that exact second.

Benefits and intended impact The biggest benefit is accessibility. Working with raw orbital data normally requires specialized software and heavy coding knowledge. We turned that complex process into something as easy to use as a weather app. The intended impact is to democratize lunar exploration—giving students, educators, and independent researchers a reliable, visually intuitive tool to plan and validate landing scenarios without getting bogged down in astrophysics math.

Tools, coding languages, and software used

  • Frontend: Built with React and Vite for a snappy, responsive user interface, and deployed on Vercel.
  • Backend: Written in Node.js and TypeScript to manage user requests, deployed on Render.
  • Database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS (hosted on Render) to store calculation history and spatial data.
  • Science Engine: A dedicated Python server using FastAPI and the SpiceyPy library to process the heavy NASA SPICE datasets.

Creativity and factors our team considered Our main creative breakthrough was the architecture. Instead of forcing heavy scientific calculations into a standard web server, we built a modern three-tier system that separates the user interface, the database management, and the intense math into three distinct parts. This keeps the website incredibly fast and prevents it from crashing when multiple people are running complex simulations.

While building, our team constantly weighed scientific accuracy against user experience. We made a strict rule never to fabricate or estimate data—if the SPICE kernels don't have the exact data for a timestamp, the app intentionally throws an error rather than guessing. We also prioritized performance, ensuring the heavy data processing happens silently in the background so the user's browser never freezes.
